Growing Up Digital:
An AI World Tour

AI isn't arriving everywhere the same way. This hour tours how it's growing up in the countries our neighbours come from, then comes home to a surprising portrait of Australia.

Figures quoted were current at their linked sources in July 2026; sentiment moves fast, so check the dates.

ntworld.inkWorkshops01 / 20
WHYthe Territory angleWhy a tour?
Why take this tour from the Northern Territory?

Nobody arrives as a blank slate

The idea

Digital worlds travel with people

When someone moves here, they bring years of experience of their home country's digital life: its platforms, its rules, its assumptions about privacy and AI. Attitudes to technology aren't just personal preferences; they're products of the systems people grew up inside.

The payoff

Meeting people where they are

The Territory's classrooms, clinics and workplaces are full of colleagues, students and clients from across Asia and beyond. Knowing what digital world someone grew up in turns generic advice into guidance that actually lands; understanding, not assumption.

The itinerary: how the world measures a country's AI readiness; a six-stop tour of homelands of some of the Territory's biggest migrant communities; what the world actually feels about AI; and then home, to what Australians really do with it.
ntworld.inkWorkshops02 / 20
KEY IDEAtwo different questionsReadiness vs sentiment
The distinction this whole hour hangs on

Is a country ready for AI, and does it want it? Different questions.

Readiness

What governments and systems can do

Measured by structured assessments: laws, institutions, skills, infrastructure, data. This is what UNESCO's Readiness Assessment Methodology evaluates, country by country. It says nothing about how people feel.

Sentiment

What people trust and fear

Measured by surveys of ordinary people: excitement, nervousness, trust in government to regulate. This is what Pew and the Stanford AI Index track. It says nothing about whether the wiring is in place.

Why it matters: the two often point in opposite directions. Some of the world's most AI-enthusiastic publics live in countries still building basic digital infrastructure, while some of the best-wired nations have the most anxious citizens. Never let one number stand in for both.
ntworld.inkWorkshops03 / 20
READINESSthe UNESCO methodMeasuring readiness
The measuring stick for our tour

UNESCO's RAM: a country-scale check-up

What it is

Readiness Assessment Methodology

A structured review a government completes with UNESCO under the global Recommendation on the Ethics of AI: legislation, institutions, skills, infrastructure and data ecosystems, ending in concrete recommendations. Dozens of countries have now published one; every report is free to read on UNESCO's Global AI Ethics and Governance Observatory.

How to read one

A mirror, not a medal

A RAM report is a self-examination, not a ranking; there's no leaderboard and no score to win. Read it for what a country says about its own gaps. (Separately, Oxford Insights publishes an annual Government AI Readiness Index that does rank countries; and the OECD has so far reviewed only a handful, so beware mislabelled citations.)

Boarding call: all six countries on our tour have completed UNESCO readiness assessments in the last two years; a quiet milestone in itself. Reports for each are on the Observatory site.
ntworld.inkWorkshops04 / 20
THE TOURfirst three stopsIndia · Bangladesh · Indonesia
The tour, first three stops

India · Bangladesh · Indonesia

India

Scale like nowhere else

Home of the world's largest digital identity system (Aadhaar) and a UNESCO readiness assessment published February 2026. Sentiment is intense both ways: 89% trust their own government to regulate AI, the highest of 25 countries Pew surveyed, yet nervousness rose 14 points in a single year, the sharpest rise recorded.

Bangladesh

The data gap, personified

Completed its UNESCO readiness assessment in November 2025 (published in draft form), yet barely features in the big global sentiment surveys. A reminder that "global" data has holes, and they're usually the same countries every time.

Indonesia

The early mover

An early adopter of UNESCO's assessment (2024), a national AI strategy since 2020, and its first comprehensive data protection law only in 2022. Daily digital life runs on WhatsApp and Grab; and its public is among the world's most upbeat, with 76% trusting their government to regulate AI.

Readiness reports: UNESCO RAM via unesco.org/ethics-ai/en/ram. Sentiment: Pew Research Center, October 2025; Stanford AI Index 2026, chapter 9 (Ipsos AI Monitor data).

ntworld.inkWorkshops05 / 20
THE TOURnext three stopsVietnam · Philippines · Thailand
The tour, next three stops

Vietnam · Philippines · Thailand

Vietnam

Assessed, but under-surveyed

Published its UNESCO readiness assessment in October 2025, one of the newest in the region; like Bangladesh, it's largely missing from the major global sentiment surveys, so its people's views go under-reported in "worldwide" headlines.

Philippines

Ethics up front

Its UNESCO assessment (November 2025) was launched under the banner of "anchoring ethics in AI governance"; a deliberate framing choice, putting values ahead of infrastructure. Filipino communities are among the Territory's largest, which makes this stop personal for many Darwin workplaces.

Thailand

Enthusiasm out front

UNESCO assessment published June 2025, and one of the world's most optimistic publics: in Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Singapore, more than 80% of people expect AI to profoundly change their lives within three to five years.

Readiness reports: UNESCO RAM via unesco.org/ethics-ai/en/ram. Sentiment: Stanford AI Index 2026, chapter 9 (Ipsos AI Monitor data).

CULTUREplatforms shape peopleDifferent worlds
What "everyone knows" isn't the same everywhere

"Just Google it" doesn't translate

·A student from China may never have used Google, YouTube, WhatsApp or ChatGPT; but they'll be expert users of WeChat, Baidu, Douyin and DeepSeek.
·An Indonesian arrival might run daily life through WhatsApp and Grab; someone from India may be entirely comfortable with Aadhaar-linked services and carry different assumptions about digital identity.
·People from countries where big AI tools were blocked or restricted often adopt them at speed on arrival; with all the enthusiasm, and none of the slowly-learned verification habits.
The teaching point: when we say "just Google it" or assume everyone's AI starting point matches ours, we may be speaking past our audience entirely. Ask what tools someone already knows; build from there.
ntworld.inkWorkshops07 / 20
CULTUREthree framings of privacyPrivacy, three ways
The deepest difference on the tour

Privacy itself is a cultural concept

Consent-based

"My data, my choice"

The Australian and broadly Western framing: privacy as an individual right, built on consent. You own your data and decide who gets access; the assumption behind our Privacy Act.

Collective-benefit

"Data serves the community"

Research on privacy attitudes in China, for example, often finds privacy framed through collective benefit and social harmony rather than individual control. Not wrong; differently reasoned.

State-managed

"The system handles it"

In government-managed digital ecosystems, people may carry quite different assumptions about who can access their data and why; and find Australian caution genuinely puzzling.

No judging on this tour: the goal isn't to rank these framings; it's to recognise that someone operating from one can find the others baffling, and that good digital-safety guidance starts from the framing a person actually holds.
ntworld.inkWorkshops08 / 20
SENTIMENTwhat the world feelsThe mood
Now the other question: what do people feel?

The world is torn, not divided

42%
The global median who feel equally concerned and excited about AI in daily life; the single most common answer across 25 countries (Pew, 28,333 adults, surveyed January to April 2025).
16%
Median who are mostly excited. No country surveyed cracked 30%. Concern leads excitement almost everywhere; around half of adults in the US, Italy, Brazil, Greece and Australia are mostly concerned.
59%
Globally, the share who say AI's benefits outweigh drawbacks, up from 55% in 2024; yet the share who say AI makes them nervous also rose, to 52% (Ipsos AI Monitor, 30 countries, via Stanford AI Index 2026).
Read those together: optimism and anxiety are rising at the same time, in the same people. That's not confusion; it's a reasonable response to a technology this large arriving this fast.
ntworld.inkWorkshops09 / 20
SENTIMENTwho's most enthusiastic?The surprise
The pattern most Australians haven't heard

The most AI-enthusiastic people aren't in the richest countries

·Southeast Asia leads the world in optimism: more than 80% in Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Singapore expect AI to profoundly change their lives in three to five years.
·Workplace adoption is higher in several emerging economies than in many advanced ones: 58% of employees globally use AI at work regularly or semi-regularly, but in India, China, Nigeria, the UAE and Saudi Arabia the share tops 80%.
·Trust in government to regulate AI runs highest in Singapore (81%) and Indonesia (76%) against a 54% global average; the United States recorded the lowest of any surveyed country, at 31%.
·Awareness runs the other way: about half of adults in Japan, Germany, France and the US have heard a lot about AI, versus 14% in India and 12% in Kenya. Enthusiasm and exposure are different things too.

Stanford AI Index 2026 chapter 9 (Ipsos AI Monitor); Pew Research Center, October 2025.

ntworld.inkWorkshops10 / 20
SENTIMENTwho should hold the leash?Trust
One more sentiment finding worth carrying home

Asked who they trust to regulate AI, the world says: the EU, then the US, then China

53%
Median trust in the European Union to regulate AI effectively, across 25 countries (Pew, 2025). The EU's early, strict AI Act appears to have bought it credibility abroad.
37%
Median trust in the United States; at home, Americans split almost evenly, 44% trusting their own country against 47% who don't.
27%
Median trust in China. Yet within many countries, people trust their own government most of all: India at 89%, Greece at just 22%.
For the Australian audience: when our government designs AI rules (see the "Australia's AI Laws" explainer on this site), it's competing for trust in a world that currently gives the benefit of the doubt to Brussels.

HOMEWARDthe Australian paradoxComing home
Last leg: bring it home

Australia: anxious in the surveys, sophisticated in practice

What surveys say

One of the wary countries

Around half of Australians say they're more concerned than excited about AI, placing us with the US, Italy, Brazil and Greece near the top of Pew's concern table. Optimism has climbed 10 points since 2022 on Ipsos's measure, but from a low base.

What behaviour says

One of the heaviest users

Anthropic's data tells a different story: Australians use Claude at more than four times the rate our population size would predict; seventh in the world per person. Wariness in surveys, enthusiasm at the keyboard.

The next few slides dig into that behavioural data: where it comes from, what Australians actually ask, and why the pattern looks encouragingly mature. Source: Anthropic, "How Australia uses Claude", 31 March 2026.
ntworld.inkWorkshops12 / 20
METHODwhere this data comes fromThe Economic Index
First, know your source; and what it reveals about metadata

How would Anthropic know?

The method

Automated analysis at scale

The Anthropic Economic Index studies aggregated, anonymised Claude.ai conversation data (this report: a February 2026 sample) to map what AI is actually used for. Its headline metric, the AI Usage Index (AUI), is simple: a place's share of usage divided by its share of population. 1.0 means "exactly proportional".

The bonus lesson

Your chats are data

Notice what this report could measure: topics, task types, complexity, even the reading level of prompts, by state. That's a window into the kind of metadata AI providers can derive from usage at scale. A good prompt for any tool you use: what does my provider's privacy policy say about how conversations are analysed?

Handle with care: this is one company's view of one assistant's users; a rich lens, not a census. It also can't see ChatGPT, Gemini or Copilot use. Treat it as directional, like every scoreboard in these workshops.

Share of Australia's Claude.ai conversations by state and territory; AUI 1.0 = proportional to population. Anthropic, February 2026 data.

The national picture

7th per person worldwide

Australia contributes 1.6% of global Claude.ai traffic (11th overall) with an AUI of 4.1. Usage splits almost evenly: 46% work, 47% personal, 7% coursework.

Reading the spread

It follows knowledge work

Only NSW and Victoria punch above their population weight. Anthropic notes the spread tracks the size of professional-service sectors, not income; adoption follows the kind of work a place does.

ntworld.inkWorkshops15 / 20
HOME DATAthe encouraging partSophistication
The finding worth celebrating

Australians are using AI like editors, not vending machines

11.9 yrs
The schooling needed to fully parse the average Australian prompt; above the global median. Australians write longer, more specified, more context-rich requests.
3.38 / 5
Australia's autonomy score: more collaborative, less delegated than the global norm. Australians iterate with the AI rather than handing work over wholesale; matching other Anglosphere countries.
2.7 hrs
Typical human-time value of tasks Australians bring to Claude, versus 3.3 hours globally: shorter but more intellectually demanding work, not bulk automation.
Why this matters for AI literacy: collaborative, well-specified, iterative use is exactly what "human in the loop" looks like in the wild. The awareness this site teaches is measurably sinking in; Australians are steering, not surrendering.

READINESSAustralia's check-upAI Agency Tool
And who's doing the readiness check-up here?

Australia's report card: the AI Agency Tool

The tool

103 capabilities, three lenses

The AI Agency Tool (Tech Policy Design Institute, final version June 2026) is a structured, repeatable method to assess a nation's AI position across 103 capabilities in six layers, scoring each for maturity, sovereignty (control, access, choice, leverage) and agency; ending in prioritised recommended actions, not just a grade.

The verdict so far

Real strengths, named gaps

Strengths: critical minerals, domain-specific datasets (medical, geospatial, environmental) and computer-vision expertise. Gaps flagged: public-sector compute, data lifecycle management, inclusive AI models and regulatory oversight capability; with a note that national planning doesn't yet fully play to Australia's strongest cards.

Close the loop: this is the same kind of self-examination UNESCO's RAM asks of the countries we toured; Australia doing its own homework, at the frontier of how AI readiness gets assessed here.
ntworld.inkWorkshops17 / 20
TAKEAWAYfive souvenirsThe takeaways
Five souvenirs from the tour

What to bring home

·Readiness and sentiment are different questions; always ask which one a headline is answering.
·Digital worlds differ; platforms, privacy framings and AI access shape people before they ever reach your classroom or counter.
·Enthusiasm lives where you least expect it; Southeast Asia leads the world in optimism, while the wealthy West worries.
·Australia is anxious in surveys and sophisticated in practice; heavy, collaborative, well-specified use. The human is staying in the loop.
·Usage data is metadata; the same reports that fascinate us should remind us to read our AI tools' privacy settings.
